# Dead-Letter Naming and Disposal Decision Record

The entry point and issues retained from the draft are still present, but the two topics were put in the same paragraph at the time, making them easy to read as the before-and-after steps of a single exception branch. This review found no evidence that ties them into a fixed sequence, so they remain recorded on the same page, with separate statements of what each is meant to answer.

## Purpose of the Early Entry

`src/Paramore.Brighter.MessagingGateway.GcpPubSub/DeadLetterPolicy.cs` is the location the earlier investigation found from the problem name and call name. It is useful for getting back to objects related to dead-letter, especially when the only clues left are "dead," "letter," "routing key," or "default."

The draft gave this entry too much weight, as if finding the file had already established the subsequent disposal relationship. This is corrected now: the path is retained only for backtracking. Name construction, caller-provided content, the default segment, changes after completion, and disposal error precedence do not automatically become related just because they appear near the same filename.

This change does not invalidate the old entry. On the contrary, the entry should remain because it explains why these two terms were initially put together. What is being removed is the reading that jumps straight from the entry to the conclusion.

## `.dlq` — the Old Clue

The early record only said `.dlq`. At the time, this helped identify the name under review, but the wording was too terse and was later easily read as "if the name ends with this suffix, dead-letter handling is already complete."

This old interpretation is now marked as no longer in use. The problem is not the suffix itself, but that it was carrying too many unstated meanings: whether the caller supplied the first part, whether the name had formed as expected, whether the result could still be processed again, and whether an error occurred during disposal. These are separate checks.

Name review therefore cannot look only at the trailing string. If an example is retained, it must at least make clear that the caller-provided portion and the default portion do not come from the same source. As for "whether it can be processed again," this version retains it only as a phenomenon to watch for when selecting a regression example; it does not present it as proof that the naming is valid.

## Review Notes

During review, two formulations were compared.

The first was to compress the page into a one-sentence process description: first obtain the dead-letter name, then interpret disposal based on that result. The benefit is brevity; the drawback is that the name and error precedence would be written as the same object.

The second was to keep only the naming and move the disposal item out. This would make the page cleaner, but would erase a real gap in the original material: the disposal issue was genuinely raised at the time, but it never became a comparison of the errors that could be recorded.

This page adopts neither extreme. The decision is to retain both topics and require new material to first identify which side it belongs to:

| Topic | Judgment retained on this page | Content it still cannot replace |
| --- | --- | --- |
| dead-letter naming | Review the name construction itself | Disposal error precedence |
| disposal error precedence | Record separately, starting from the pre-call state | Checking the name suffix |
| `DeadLetterPolicy.cs` | The old troubleshooting entry point | A summary of the call relationship |

The third row is there to prevent the old misreading from recurring. A file entry point can restart troubleshooting, but it cannot by itself answer "which error remains" or "which parts make up the name."

## An Arrangement That Left No Result Recorded

At one point, the plan was to inspect the name first and then disposal in the same pass. This plan left no usable result on record, so it cannot serve as evidence of an ordering relationship.

However, it exposed the draft's conflation. On the naming side, what is actually needed is a short example that distinguishes caller content from the default portion; on the disposal side, what is actually needed is the pre-call state and whether there were any additional changes after completion. Both can be viewed in the same work window, but each must leave its own result.

The original note treated "whether the result can still be processed again" as a shared check. It is now split by question: on the naming side, it only serves as a reminder not to hide the subsequent-processing state in the selected example; on the disposal side, it cannot substitute for error precedence. This revision does not claim that reprocessing has already yielded any particular result.

## Retained Old Conclusion

> Seeing `.dlq` means this part of dead-letter handling is complete.

This statement remains here, marked as **deprecated**. It was convenient shorthand, but it collapsed the name's visible form and disposal completion into a single judgment. If the same legacy regression is encountered again, first check whether it only compared the suffix.

Another old statement was "Naming is determined first, and disposal errors naturally come later." This is no longer applicable either. It does not say which action "determined first" refers to, or whether "later" means when the error appears, is saved, or is observed. Without those reference points, sequencing words only create a sense of certainty.

## Decision Boundary for This Version

Naming issues continue to be handled as naming issues; disposal error precedence remains a separate confirmation item. A follow-up note that only points to the same file again without saying which item it supplements must not be written as a new conclusion.

The disposal side still lacks a minimal reproduction: what state existed before the call, whether there were any additional changes after completion, and whether those changes are actually related to retaining the error. Leave the gap here; do not rewrite it as default behavior.

# Dead-Letter Naming and Disposal Decision Record

This record spans several rounds of reliability train consolidation. Initially, there was only a path, a shorthand note about `.dlq`, and a disposal question whose ordering had not been settled; later, reviewers split up the shorthand note, and the review arrangements left further gaps where nothing had been written back. The old paragraphs are still retained below, because this page's value lies not only in stating the final naming requirement, but also in explaining which seemingly convenient inferences can no longer be used.

The page has consistently focused on two local topics: dead-letter naming and disposal error precedence. The former concerns how the name of RoutingKey is constructed, while the latter concerns the order in which errors are retained during disposal. They were once included in the same round of finalization, and the earlier investigation could start from the same local entry point; this explains why they are on the same page, but is not enough to combine them into a single operational conclusion.

## 2023-04-19: The Initially Recorded Entry Point

The earliest version did not try to describe the full process. It left only `src/Paramore.Brighter.MessagingGateway.GcpPubSub/DeadLetterPolicy.cs` and recorded the two questions alongside the path separately: one was how to trace back the name of dead-letter, and the other was where to start reproducing disposal error precedence.

The material available at the time was sparse. `.dlq` was recorded as an easily recognizable fragment, while the rest of the name was not clearly recorded; the disposal item only called for starting with the state before the call and recording any additional changes separately after completion. The first draft did not list the errors to be compared, nor did it state that any particular error took precedence.

Two limitations at this stage remained worth retaining later. First, the path is a starting point for tracing back, not a determination of implementation ownership. Second, naming results cannot substitute for disposal observations. The early author put both things on the same page to keep the train materials from becoming scattered, not to claim that they belonged to the same rule.

The first draft also contained an obviously inadequate shorthand: seeing `.dlq` led to a tendency to interpret the dead-letter side as "already handled". No one elaborated on that statement at the time, so readers could not know whether "handled" referred to name formation, the message's subsequent state, or disposal having finished. The early versions did not fill this gap with an answer.

## The Old Working Hypothesis from 2023

The early notes once used a convenient working hypothesis: since the name already carried the dead-letter ending, disposal probably just continued after naming. This hypothesis spread easily because it arranged the two terms into a sentence that read smoothly.

It left no call boundary. Without a boundary, we cannot determine which action the so-called "after" follows, nor the point at which the disposal error occurs, is propagated, or is saved. At the time, no evidence supported a more fine-grained ordering, so this passage should be treated only as a working hypothesis and should not be backfilled as a historically established rule.

The old hypothesis was not deleted. It explains why later reviews repeatedly encounter the same misreading: some infer a disposal error from the end of the name, while others infer a naming rule from "can still be processed again." Both readings fill in an intermediate relationship that was never recorded.

## 2024-01-25: Split After Review

The second version first addressed the ambiguities in the document, rather than fabricating a run result. The review conclusion was: name construction and error priority should each retain their own questions, examples, and locations for follow-up notes.

The questions on the naming side are more specific: where the caller-provided content is, where the default portion is, and how the final name is identified. The questions on the disposal side are different: reproduction should begin with the state before the call, and whether there are any additional changes after completion should be recorded separately; if multiple errors exist in the future, it must first be made clear which errors are being compared.

This split changed the status of the old entry point. `DeadLetterPolicy.cs` remains a common starting point for historical troubleshooting, especially when old records contain only dead-letter, routing key, or terms like default. It is no longer treated as proof that all relationships have been found. The path name cannot indicate disposal priority, nor can it explain the caller's template.

The review also eliminated a shortcut check: checking only `.dlq`. A suffix can help identify the default segment, but by itself cannot show whether the name preserves the caller's intent. If a regression shows only the trailing string, it can still serve as an old example, but it should not bear the full naming judgment.

## Old Proposal Retained in Place

> As long as the name ends with `.dlq`, subsequent disposal can be understood as following the same path.

This passage was **later overturned; original text retained**.

It compresses the name's appearance, caller-provided content, reprocessing, and disposal errors into a single "same path." It looks convenient when written, but during review it is impossible to tell what exactly was validated. A name can have a default suffix, but that does not mean disposal has completed; changes may occur after completion, but that does not mean it is known which error should be retained.

The motivation behind the old proposal is understandable: at the time, the aim was to cover the adjacent issues in the reliability train with a single short sentence. Its merged conclusion is no longer adopted, but the same-page arrangement is retained. Adjacent issues can be navigated together, but the bases for judgment cannot be merged.

Another old note reads "Determine naming first; errors naturally come later." This statement is likewise no longer valid. It does not define whether "determine" means name concatenation, message delivery, or the return of some call; nor does it define whether "later" means temporal order or the order in which exceptions are presented. A sequencing term with no defined object is insufficient to constitute a disposal decision.

## A Review Plan That Was Not Completed

In the earlier records, there was a plan to include both topics in the same review: first look at the name, then at disposal. The plan did not yield any results that could be written back. Here, that gap is not recast as experimental success, failure, or incident recovery; it only indicates that there was no material at the time to link the two observations into a causal chain.

However, this plan did leave two clear places for follow-up notes.

The naming side needs an example short enough for reviewers to distinguish the caller-provided part from the default part, rather than just see the suffix. The disposal side needs to preserve the pre-call state and, after completion, record whether any additional changes occurred. The same work window can trigger both, but a result on one side does not serve as evidence for the other.

"Whether the result can still be processed again" also came up in this plan. It was later reframed as a background condition for the naming example: this phenomenon can be considered when selecting an example, but it cannot by itself establish that name construction is correct, much less answer the question of disposal error precedence. This revision makes no claim about what result reprocessing produced; it only moves it out of the wrong place.

## Two remarks left in the review margins

There is a brief note beside the review materials:

> First ask whether you are looking at the name or at disposal errors.

This sentence did not become a behavioral rule, but it changed how the material was read afterward. Only by first identifying the subject can we avoid borrowing the meaning of "default" in a name to explain error handling, or retroactively turning a particular disposal observation into a naming rule.

The other note says: a file path can be an entry point, not a conclusion. It preserves a specific way to use the path: the earlier investigation can be resumed from `src/Paramore.Brighter.MessagingGateway.GcpPubSub/DeadLetterPolicy.cs`; what to verify next should be determined by the subject currently being pursued. For naming, check the components of the name; for disposal, check the pre-call state and the changes after completion.

Both notes are narrower in scope than "a unified review of the dead-letter process". The latter would make even undocumented relationships appear to have already been covered, while the former merely prevent the old combined interpretation from expanding further.

## 2025-09: The naming side re-enters the train

RLY-201 brought dead-letter naming back into regression checks. The card's work was aimed at selecting the shortest real example from the existing regressions and checking whether the result could still be processed again. The public contract name it used was `DeadLetterNamingConvention`, so this page retains that name as the navigation label for the naming side.

The card first moved to In Progress, then became blocked. The reason for the block was that reproduction needed to wait until after the Transport contracts release window. This change explains why new review results were not immediately written back to this page, but it provides neither the final form of the name nor the ordering for disposal error precedence.

After the card was reintroduced, an ambiguity in the earlier text became more apparent. Previously, when we wrote "reproduction complete", we did not distinguish whether what had been completed was the check of the naming example or the confirmation of the disposal error. The two are now recorded separately: RLY-201 corresponds to navigation for the shortest naming example; disposal issues remain at their own entry points and record locations.

On the naming side, having a navigation label does not mean we can check only keywords. The purpose of the regression example is to place the caller portion and the default portion within the same identifiable name construction, not to replace an assessment of their construction relationship with a single string search.

## 2025-10: The disposal item remains a separate entry point

RLY-217 keeps disposal error precedence in a separate maintenance entry point. Its pending task starts from the pre-call state and requires confirmation of whether any additional visible changes remain after completion. What can be confirmed here is that this item has still not been subsumed by the naming conclusion; the pending task itself does not establish which error should take precedence.

This is also why this page retains unresolved items. If a future reproduction involves multiple errors, the record needs to state which objects actually participate in the comparison, at which disposal boundary the observation occurs, and whether the post-completion changes are related to error retention. Until these details are available, writing a particular order as the default would recreate the linear narrative that the earlier documentation had already corrected.

There is still one sufficiently narrow connection between naming and disposal: both are limited-scope material for the reliability train, and both can be traced back further from a specific calling context. Beyond that, any stronger connection must be established by subsequent records, not created by the page's side-by-side layout.

## Most recent correction

The most recent feedback from the field called for correcting the earlier assessment. What was corrected was not an already archived execution output, but the wording in the document that casually presented name construction as a prerequisite for disposal.

The old wording first assumed a fixed linear order, then slotted `.dlq`, caller content, post-completion changes, and error precedence into that order. This could mislead readers into thinking that once the name was identified, the conclusion about disposal was already available.

The revised wording is narrower: names answer only naming questions; disposal errors answer only disposal-error questions. If future material proves that a particular call site makes the two adjacent, that call site itself should be recorded, rather than using "adjacency" as a substitute for causality. If a reproduction touches on both items, it should also state separately which part of name construction and which part of disposal observation it covers.

This correction has not changed the earlier plan's goal of reducing fragmentation in the records. The page still retains two topics and two navigation directions; what has been abandoned is the approach of blurring boundaries for the sake of consolidation.

## Current naming requirements

After the initial record, the split during review, the unfinished recheck, the review comments, and the reintroduction of RLY-201, the naming section is now consolidated here into the current requirements:

DeadLetterNamingConvention formats a RoutingKey with a caller template and the default .dlq suffix.

This sentence addresses only how the name is composed. The caller template is not optional background information, and the default `.dlq` suffix cannot stand in for the entire name on its own. When choosing the shortest real example for RLY-201, both parts should be identifiable; an old example showing only the suffix is not a sufficient example for the current requirement.

The diagram below shows only the objects that need to be revisited together during the naming review, not the execution order of disposal:

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Review
    state "Naming review" as Review
    state "caller template" as Template
    state "default .dlq suffix" as Suffix
    state "RoutingKey" as Key
    Review --> Template
    Review --> Suffix
    Template --> Key
    Suffix --> Key
    Key --> [*]
```

The old path can still be retained as a historical entry point, but it does not replace this requirement. The path helps readers find the local object again; the current requirement preserves the relationship in which both the caller template and the default suffix must contribute to the name.

## Decision boundary for disposal error precedence

This page's decision on the disposal item is: do not infer error precedence from the naming requirement, and do not present the still-unconfirmed statement that "there may be additional changes after completion" as established behavior.

This does not move the issue off this page. RLY-217 remains the maintenance entry point on the disposal side, and reproduction should still begin from the state before the call. If disposal records become available in the future, they should first state the observed boundaries; if there are multiple errors, they should then specify which errors are being compared. Only once such material is available is there a reason to add the precedence itself.

Therefore, any conclusion this page currently permits must avoid inventing a default order. The historical claim that "disposal naturally follows completion of the name" is no longer valid and cannot be reintroduced with more formal wording. The naming issue has a clear requirement; the disposal issue is still waiting for records of its own.

## Adjacent issues not yet split out

The disposal items still contain several points that must not be removed: how the pre-call state should be preserved, whether any additional changes actually occur after completion, and which objects need to be compared if multiple errors occur. They are directly adjacent to RLY-217, and keeping them here helps prevent readers from assuming that the naming requirements already cover disposal.

There is also a related but smaller issue on the naming side: the "can still be processed again" check in the shortest real example should remain within that example's context. It can help select regression cases, but it cannot replace identifying the caller template and default suffix, nor can it be stretched beyond its scope to explain error precedence.

The two issues should not be combined into "dead-letter has been verified". That would once again collapse a settled naming requirement and a disposal observation that has yet to be recorded into the same status.

## Old Examples Appendix

### A. Checking Only the Suffix

Old examples are often written as "you can stop once you see `.dlq`". This example is outdated because it does not show the caller template. It is retained to identify narrow checks in older regression cases: if an example has only the suffix and no caller portion, it cannot represent the current naming requirements.

### B. Using Reprocessing to Answer Questions About Error Ordering

Another old example places "whether the result can still be processed again" at the end of disposal error precedence, as if that explains which error should be retained. That example is also no longer applicable. Reprocessing appears in the naming review context of RLY-201 and cannot automatically serve as the answer to the error comparison required by RLY-217.

### C. The Old Reading That Starts at the Entry Point

Early troubleshooting would start from `DeadLetterPolicy.cs` and then lump all dead-letter questions into the same section because the issue names were similar. It is still possible to start here, but the checks should be separated as soon as you reach the local object: when checking names, look at the caller template and default suffix; when checking disposal, look at the pre-call state and post-completion changes. The entry point is still valid, but the combined reading is no longer valid.

If the next follow-up note comes from RLY-201, it should be recorded on the naming side, explaining whether the example shows both the caller template and the default suffix. If it comes from RLY-217, it should be recorded on the disposal side, explaining the pre-call state, post-completion changes, and the actual error objects compared. Do not fold the two follow-up notes back into a single broad statement of closure.

# Invalid Route Call Recording Proposal

For this round, do not combine invalid route naming and processor call recording into a single change. The two are adjacent at the interface, but when a failure occurs, it must be possible to distinguish whether the naming choice is wrong or the call record ended up in an inappropriate place.

The initial draft assumed that the area near the mapper was enough to hold both route naming and the recording entry point. The tentative plan is to first make a limited comparison of two options.

- Option A: Generate the invalid route name in the same place, and leave the processor call record there.
- Option B: Keep naming only on the mapping side; handle recording on the processor call side.

A keeps the read path short; its downside is that once recording affects the caller's judgment, the naming issue will be pulled into the investigation along with it. B has a clearer change boundary, but whether the caller can obtain the same message context still needs to be confirmed.

The tentative preference is B. The withdrawal condition is straightforward: if the call side has to re-derive the route name in order to record it, do not maintain the split; that would turn one clearly defined naming task into two separate guesses.

The verification entry point is provisionally noted as `src/Paramore.Brighter.Transformers.MassTransit/MassTransitMessageMapper.cs`. The local mapping-related objects can be seen here; whether naming ultimately belongs here remains to be reviewed. The format, timing, and content to retain for processor call recording have also not been decided.

# Invalid Route Call Recording Proposal

The initial draft treated the area near the mapper as the common location for both issues; that assessment is withdrawn. After review, `src/Paramore.Brighter.Transformers.MassTransit/MassTransitMessageMapper.cs` is suitable as an entry point for locating invalid route naming, but its file location alone cannot establish that it should handle processor call recording. Accordingly, the previous Option A is no longer the default direction.

The remaining issue is not "whether to record"; it is that recording cannot take on the explanatory responsibility for naming. If a processor call record only proves that the call occurred, it still cannot show what route name the invalid message ultimately used; conversely, even stable naming examples cannot replace checking the call location. The two pieces of material should be readable separately.

This round proposes a narrower trial path: first limit the naming issue to the route name produced for invalid messages, then separately organize the recording location for processor calls. Neither side is required to become a unified entry point. This adds one additional comparison, but avoids putting unconfirmed responsibility for the call in the same place.

The two original candidate options are rewritten as follows.

| Candidate | Content retained | Content not yet committed |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Mapping-side naming | Rules and examples for invalid route names | Do not use this to infer the processor's recording responsibility |
| Call-side recording | The location of processor calls and the recording requirements | Do not recalculate invalid route names |
| Merged implementation | Consider it only after both sides confirm the same naming context | Not included in the trial at this point |

The cost is that review has to cover two types of snippets instead of a single change. The benefit is that counterexamples are easier to localize: if the route name does not match expectations, go back to the mapping side first; if the name is correct but the processor call was not recorded, check the call side. Do not reclassify the latter case as a naming-rule failure.

There are two conditions for withdrawing the trial. First, the call side cannot obtain the naming context needed to distinguish invalid messages and can only copy the mapping logic. Second, the mapping side starts depending on processor call details in order to write the record. If either occurs, revisit the comparison with a merged approach, but first list the overlapping context; ownership cannot be decided solely because "code is closer."

Unconfirmed items: which object should hold the record; whether all processor calls need the same handling; whether the existing examples of invalid route names cover the actual integration paths. Do not mark the mapper as the sole owner until the latter two are decided.

# Invalid Route Call Recording Proposal

This note originally framed the issue as "add a recording point next to the mapper." That wording made discussion easier, but collapsed two distinct decisions into one: what route name an invalid message should get, and where a processor call should be recorded. The later review did not establish that file location alone gave those two decisions a shared home.

Option A, retained from the earlier draft, handles naming and recording in the same place. Its only appeal is that the changes look localized. The drawbacks are also clear: when a record is missing, investigators will suspect naming first; when a name is wrong, they will pull the processor call path into the investigation. This option remains here as a consolidation approach we considered, but we no longer recommend trying it as-is.

## Boundaries retained from the review

`src/Paramore.Brighter.Transformers.MassTransit/MassTransitMessageMapper.cs` is still the starting point for investigating this issue. It puts the objects relevant to invalid route naming in a traceable location and provides a starting point for revisiting mapping-side decisions. It does not automatically settle where processor call recording belongs; a filename, adjacent declarations, and a single call-name match are no substitute for the call relationships themselves.

So the review no longer asks "which file handles both things," but instead asks two smaller questions.

1. Whether the naming rules for invalid messages already yield stable, verifiable results on the mapping side.
2. Whether processor call recording can stay on the calling side without duplicating or guessing the naming rules.

The second question is not a secondary check on the naming rules. If the recording location needs to regenerate the name, it creates a second set of rules; if recording requirements drive changes to names, the original routing problem loses its independent failure signal.

## Current trial

The proposal uses separate supporting materials and separate changes. First, lock down the naming convention for invalid-message routes, then find a location for processor call recording that does not recompute the name. The two can appear side by side in review, but "a change in the same place" is not a completion criterion.

The naming convention is: InvalidMessageNamingConvention emits the .invalid suffix for invalid-message routes.

This statement covers only the naming result. It does not prescribe a structure for the record or say that every processor call must produce the same record. Previously, folding undecided points like these into the naming discussion made it hard to tell whether examples were validating names or calls.

The trial requirement on the recording side is narrower: records should correspond to actual processor calls, not derive a new routing rule by working backward from the mapping result. Review materials need to show which call site the recording is adjacent to; if the only way to guess whether a call occurred is from the name string, the recording proposal is not yet on solid ground. There is no requirement here to handle all calls in one format; the immediate priority is to avoid reinterpreting the objects being named.

Splitting the work makes the changes look less compact than a single-location approach. The cost is having to read the naming and call snippets separately. We chose this not out of a preference for layering, but because the two failure modes each need their own starting point: when the name is wrong, revisit the naming rules first; when the name is correct but there is no call record, revisit the recording location. That way, a problem in one place does not lead to changes in the other before its involvement has been confirmed.

## Consolidation approaches not being adopted

We considered attaching recording directly near the mapper and treating it as part of the naming checks. That approach is now retained only for comparison: it fits when the two concerns truly share the same context. The review has not established that premise, so it is not the default implementation path.

Another overly aggressive approach is to have the calling side reconstruct invalid route naming itself. That makes recording self-contained, but creates two sets of naming decisions. They may agree in the short term, but after one is adjusted, it becomes difficult to determine where a difference came from. We will not take that route unless the split approach is shown to require passing context that cannot be obtained.

To reopen the merged approach, at least one specific condition must first be met: the calling side cannot identify invalid messages without deriving their names; or the mapping side must depend on processor call details to preserve the existing naming. At that point, the comparison should focus on that missing context, not on "which file is closer to the problem."

## Materials for the next review

- Keep the existing examples of invalid-message naming separate from existing processor call records, so a single example does not have to support two decisions.
- Confirm whether the calling side can identify the required message context; if not, state exactly what is missing rather than directly copying the naming logic.
- Check whether missing records could be misreported as route-name problems.
- If a proposal to merge the two comes up, show the duplicated context it eliminates, rather than just saying the changes will be more localized.

The granularity of the recorded content is still undecided, and the mapper has not been designated as the sole home for processor calls. This draft only tightens the naming convention and separates the two types of review; if clear call relationships are established later, we can then decide whether the recording location needs to change.

# Rejection Value and Warning Triage Tree

When a report says "the rejection reason is wrong," first distinguish whether the caller has a rejection object or text that has already been displayed. Currently, collect only two directly observable results: the reason value and whether the description is empty. If the two did not come from the same read, do not combine them into a complete object.

Keep pipeline warnings in a separate section. Appearing alongside a rejection report does not mean they came from the same part of processing. First record whether the warning was seen before, during, or after processing; if its location is unclear, retain the original observation without adding an exception type.

```text
Incident report
├─ Rejection object available
│  ├─ Record the reason value
│  ├─ Record the description or empty value
│  ├─ Identify the source of the read
│  └─ Record displayed text separately
├─ Only displayed text available
│  └─ Go back to the caller that produced the text
└─ Only a warning available
   ├─ Record where it was observed
   └─ Do not fill in rejection fields
```

The old habit was to assume that the value had not changed whenever reason text was visible. This is only a rough way to sort samples during collection: the display layer may not show the description, or may add text of its own. If the description is empty, do not substitute a warning or UI text for it.

Start by recording source-code reading notes in `src/Paramore.Brighter/CommandProcessor.cs`. The `CommandProcessor` in that file is an entry point to revisit; we cannot yet determine which path a warning belongs to from an exception name, or conclude from a throw site in the file that the rejection object's fields have changed.

If an incident report includes both a warning and some exception text, first treat them as two separate pieces of evidence. If the exception text does not state where the object was read from, do not use it as a substitute for the reason value or description.

# Troubleshooting Tree for Rejection Values and Warning Partitions

This review starts by separating two kinds of reports that have long been mixed together: one says the rejection value has "changed shape"; the other only says a pipeline warning appeared at an unexpected point. The old draft put them under the same exception path to make it easier to collect similar observations. There is no evidence that a warning is constructed from a rejection object, or that exception text or display text can stand in for object fields.

```text
Collected evidence
│
├─ Rejection object available
│  ├─ Reason value and description come from the same read
│  │  ├─ Retain the reason value
│  │  ├─ Record an empty description as empty
│  │  ├─ Record display text separately as a caller-visible observation
│  │  └─ Then check whether the caller performed a conversion
│  ├─ Only display text is available
│  │  ├─ Return to the entry point that produced the text
│  │  └─ Stop attributing field behavior until an object read is confirmed
│  └─ The two values come from different records
│     └─ Save as two samples; do not combine them
│
└─ Only a pipeline warning is visible
   ├─ Record whether it was before, during, or after processing
   ├─ Check whether a rejection object is available from the same case
   ├─ No object: continue from the warning's location
   ├─ Object available: still save them separately first
   └─ Location unknown: stop at data collection or the caller entry point
```

## 2023-03-20: Old Guidance

Initially, this was framed as a display-layer issue: if the reason value could be displayed, the rejection value was provisionally treated as normal; if the description was not displayed, it was assumed that the accompanying text had not been passed through. This framing helped with early searches because most reports at the time left only a single line of output, with no record of an object read.

The problem was that it collapsed three different cases into one: the description was already empty in the object; the caller received the object but did not display the description; or the display layer added default text of its own. Looking only at the final text, all three look like "the description is missing." The old wording is still here to keep this page searchable under the original terms for older callers; it is no longer a criterion for considering field checks complete.

The old page also said, "When a warning appears near a rejection, handle it as a rejection first." That was the working assumption at the time. Ordering in the logs only establishes the order of observation; it does not prove that the warning and the rejection object were produced by the same processing logic. When revisiting these older samples, first look for an object read, then decide which branch to take.

## Stop Points Added by the On-Call Notes

The initial note only said, "If there's an object, record the reason and description." Later, this proved insufficient: a reason value could come from an object read while the description came from another log entry or a displayed result. Each value could look reasonable on its own, yet together they would not make up a single sample.

So the read source was added as an item to record. Keep the reason value and description in the same object record only when they come from the same object; if they come from different places, save them separately and label their sources. Without a shared read source, do not mark the record as a "complete rejection value."

Warnings have a similar gap. Older records often only said "saw a warning," without specifying which part of processing it occurred in. Later readers cannot tell whether it was a signal already present before processing, a signal that appeared during processing, or text seen by the caller after processing ended. An unknown location does not mean the warning is invalid; it only means this page cannot take the attribution any further.

## An Attempt to Trace Back by Exception Name

During the review, tracing back from exception names led to `src/Paramore.Brighter/CommandProcessor.cs`. This file can be used to locate `namespace Paramore.Brighter` and `public partial class CommandProcessor : IAmACommandProcessor`; it also shows where throws occur near `throw new ArgumentException(` and a navigation point for `InvalidOperationException`.

This reading did not identify the warning's source. Exception types can narrow the scope of reading, but cannot assign the warning to any one of these exception paths; exception messages are not the reason value or description in the rejection object. In the old notes, "found the exception name" was written too much like a conclusion. It is now treated as an entry point for reading the source code.

If the available evidence consists only of an exception type, part of a stack trace, or error text with no known source, first retain that entry point and the original text. Do not classify the report as a rejection-value issue or a warning-partition issue just because the file contains `ArgumentException` or `InvalidOperationException`.

## The Transaction Lead That Went Off Track

The same file also contains `public static Type GetTransactionTypeFromTransactionProvider (IAmABoxTransactionProvider? transactionProvider)` and the binding location for `transactionProviderInterface`. Early reviews treated this section as the next step in tracing the value's shape, simply because it was adjacent to an exception reference point.

The source reading so far does not support that direction. What can be confirmed here is that functions related to the transaction provider type exist; it cannot be confirmed that they define the shape of rejection values, or that they affect where warnings are observed. A transaction provider, an exception name, and a rejection report may all appear in the same case, but that does not make them a causal chain.

This lead was not removed from the old page because some people search for transactions, exceptions, and rejections together. Its only remaining use is as a reminder: when you see nearby type-related functions, do not let source-code location stand in for object-read results. Do not pursue this line further without new evidence from callers.

## 2023-10-25: Classification After Review

When a rejection object is available, record the reason value, description, and read source. Keep the empty value if the description is empty; display text may be retained, but it must be labeled as a caller-visible observation. When only display text is available, return to the entry point that generates the text, and do not enumerate possible causes of field changes until an object read has been confirmed.

When only a pipeline warning is available, first record where it was observed. If there is no object from the same case, continue investigating at the warning's location; if an object is supplied later, do not rewrite the old warning record as object fields. The two types of evidence can appear side by side, but each retains its original source.

This classification does not explain all differences between callers. It only avoids two common shortcuts: inferring object fields from display text, and inferring a processing relationship from the proximity of a warning and a rejection. If the next review obtains an object read and display output from the same entry point, then determine whether the difference arises in the object, during conversion, or at the display stage.

# Rejection Value and Warning Partition Troubleshooting Tree

When rejection value shape and pipeline warning partition are reported together from an incident, do not start by choosing a single shared exception name. First check which category the material at hand falls into: whether a rejection object was actually read, whether the reason value and description came from the same read, and where in processing the warning was observed. The older records contain several quicker classification methods, which are still retained below; they explain why older callers find their way here, and why the current troubleshooting tree has additional stop conditions.

```text
Report received
│
├─ Rejection object available
│  ├─ Reason value and description come from the same read
│  │  ├─ Save both read results
│  │  ├─ Description is empty: leave it empty
│  │  ├─ Record display text separately as an observation at the caller
│  │  └─ Proceed to object inspection
│  ├─ Only display text is available
│  │  ├─ Return to the caller that generated the text
│  │  └─ Stop attributing fields until an object read is confirmed
│  └─ Reason value and description come from different records
│     └─ Save them separately, do not combine them into a single object sample
│
└─ Only pipeline warning is available
   ├─ Indicate whether the observation was before processing, during processing or after processing
   ├─ Check whether a rejection object is also available from the same incident
   ├─ No object: investigate based on the location of the warning
   ├─ Object available: still record the two types of signals separately
   └─ Location unknown: stop at collection or the caller entry point
```

This tree does not require every branch to be followed every time. Its purpose is to prevent an incomplete report from being filled in using another nearby piece of material. Object reads, formatted text, exception snippets and the locations where warning is observed, each support different conclusions. A report can be short, as long as it retains the piece of evidence it actually has.

## 2023-03-20: The Original Notes

The original notes treated "the value has the wrong shape" as a display issue. The wording at the time was straightforward: if the reason value could be displayed, provisionally classify it as normal; if the description was not displayed, temporarily treat it as missing accompanying text. This was written to group similar reports together, since most of the material at hand at the time consisted of single lines of output, with almost no records of object reads.

This assessment has not been removed. It still serves as a small reminder for older incidents with only a piece of formatted text: do not infer the reason value from a single line of text. But it can no longer serve as a condition for completing the check. The display component may ignore an empty description, may insert a default sentence itself, or may not have read the same object at all; "a reason is visible on the screen" is not enough to distinguish these cases.

There was another quicker approach at the time: if a warning appeared close to a rejection symptom, provisionally classify it under the rejection flow. That was only a working hypothesis, not a confirmed relationship. The ordering in the logs indicates at most the order of observation, it cannot prove that the warning and the rejection object were constructed by the same section of processing, much less show that the text in the warning can be used to fill in the description.

The value of the early records is that they preserve the entry-point terms used at the time. When legacy callers find this page by searching for "reason display", "rejection prompt", or warning, they should first see that these terms are outdated, then return to the branches for the object and the observation location. Simply deleting the old sentences would cause similar old reports to be misclassified again.

## A stopping point noted in the margin that same day

The margin note in the first draft said only, "If there is an object, record the reason and description; if there is no object, do not fill in fields." It later became clear that the note was missing a key condition: whether the reason value and description came from the same read. A reason value may come from the object, while the description comes from another log, the display layer, or another execution. Each may look reasonable on its own, but together they do not constitute a single object sample.

Therefore, later records no longer recorded just the two fields, but also the read source. Only when both results come from the same object read are they placed under the same object record. If the sources differ, keep them as two separate pieces of evidence and make it clear that they have not yet been linked. This stopping point leaves some reports temporarily without a conclusion about "whether the rejection value has changed", but it preserves distinctions that can be verified.

The margin notes about warning have the same problem. A common wording on old pages was "saw a warning", without specifying whether it appeared before, during, or after processing. Without that location, later readers cannot determine whether it was a signal during processing or text the caller saw after already receiving the processing result. An unknown location is not a reason to arbitrarily assign an exception type.

At the time, some people preferred to map warning to the rejection entry point first, then go back to look for the object. This order seemed fast when only sequential logs were available, but it mistakes the observation order for a processing relationship. When encountering this old recommendation now, first confirm whether an object read was actually recorded in the same observed context; if not, you cannot follow the rejection branch to label warning.

## A review of samples with only display text remaining

Reports collected later did not always provide an object. Some callers left only the final displayed text, which contained fragments of the reason or description but did not identify the object that produced it, the conversion location, or the read time. The old approach copied this text directly into the "reason value" column, then filled in the description using the default sentence in the UI.

This approach is now marked as deprecated. Display text is what the caller ultimately presents, not the equivalent of an object read. It may omit an empty description, replace words, or combine multiple sources. When only display text is available, return to the caller entry point that generated the text; until an object read is confirmed, stop judging whether the enum value or description has changed.

Stopping field attribution does not mean stopping the investigation. This branch can still preserve the text as-is, the location where it appeared, and the caller entry point. If object read results are obtained later, add the new evidence alongside the existing evidence rather than backfilling the old text as field values. This makes it possible to see whether differences come from the object itself, the conversion from object to text, or the final display.

This is especially true when the description is empty. An empty value is an actual observation, and the fact that the final UI displays a sentence does not mean that text can be treated as the object's description. Supplemental text from the display layer should remain in the displayed result and must not overwrite the earlier empty-value record.

## 2023-10-25: Trace back by exception name

An earlier review started with exception names, trying to explain warning partitioning through throw sites. Reading the code led to `src/Paramore.Brighter/CommandProcessor.cs`. Here, `namespace Paramore.Brighter`, `public partial class CommandProcessor : IAmACommandProcessor`, and the throw sites near `throw new ArgumentException(` can be located; the same file also provides a location for `InvalidOperationException`.

This attempt did not identify the source of the warning. Exception types can narrow the scope of code reading, but they cannot assign the warning to one of those exception paths. Exception messages also cannot substitute for the rejection object's reason value or description. Earlier notes made "seeing an exception name" sound almost like a conclusion, and that wording has now been revised: exception names are only suitable as starting points for follow-up investigation.

This failed attempt left behind a useful rule. If the available incident evidence provides only an exception type, a small portion of the stack, or error text with no stated source, do not choose a "rejection value" or "warning partition" for it. Preserve the entry point and the original observations, and wait for the object to be read or for the location where the warning was observed to be identified. This will not make the report complete immediately, but it will keep the next round of code reading from going down the wrong branch.

The presence of `CommandProcessor` in the file also does not mean that this type handles all nearby observations. It is only a local navigation aid available for the current follow-up investigation. After reading an exception throw site, you must still return to the incident evidence to confirm: whether the reporter obtained the object, and where the warning was observed. Without these two items, proximity in the source code cannot fill in incident facts.

This is also where older troubleshooting records are easy to misread. Issue names and call names lead readers to the same file, and the file does indeed contain exception locations, making it easy to treat "can be located" as "has been attributed". The two are not the same thing. The file path is retained here so that those who need to read the code have a starting point; it is not intended to tie the warning partition to a particular exception.

## The transaction lead that went off track during the same review

You can also locate `public static Type GetTransactionTypeFromTransactionProvider (IAmABoxTransactionProvider? transactionProvider)` in the same file, and find the binding location for `transactionProviderInterface`. Early review work treated this section as the next hop for investigating the value's shape, on the grounds that it was near the exception locations and also involved types.

That direction was later abandoned. The available material only supports "there is a function here related to the transaction provider type", not "it determines the rejection value shape", nor "it explains where the warning was observed". There is no documented direct connection between the function's visible location and the ownership of the object's fields.

Transaction providers, exception types, and rejection reports can all appear in the same incident. When you encounter this combination, first finish reading the object and recording the warning's location; list the transaction provider observations separately. Do not establish a causal relationship among them in the same conclusion, and do not use inferences based on the transaction type to override object results that have already been obtained.

This old lead remains in the document because people searching for "transaction", "exception", or "rejection" often end up here. Its purpose is now very narrow: to remind readers that another type-related function visible in the file is not a fallback entry point for this page's troubleshooting tree. Without material from a direct caller, do not continue extending the speculation by following that function.

## 2023-10-26: Boundaries left by the review

The review narrowed the records back down to two minimal questions. The first was whether the caller obtained the rejection object, and whether the reason value and description came from the same read. The second was where in processing the warning was observed, and whether a rejection object was also present in the same context.

This review did not require every report to become a complete analysis. It targeted two common leaps: inferring object fields from displayed text, and inferring causality from a warning appearing next to a rejection. The former conflates an empty description, a description that is not displayed, and default text; the latter makes the warning's observation point disappear from the record.

The actions following the review were very specific. When an object is available, first record both read results and their sources; when only displayed text is available, stop at the caller that produced the text. When only a warning is available, first record the observation point; when that point is unclear, stop at the collection entry point or the caller entry point. Stopping does not mean declaring the report invalid, but rather not filling in its gaps with text from another path.

The review retained an earlier recommendation: "When you see a warning, search the rejection entry point first." This is useful only when a rejection object has already been confirmed in the same context. Without an object, searching the rejection entry point often finds only seemingly relevant exception snippets, and still does not reveal where the warning was observed. It was therefore moved from the first step to after object confirmation.

Another retained trace of the review is the requirement for record granularity. The object and warning can be included in the same incident report, but they cannot share a set of fields. Object records belong under value shape, while warning records belong under processing location. When both types of material are present, the report may at most note that they appeared in the same context, and neither may be treated as the source of the other.

## Partial corrections to the old troubleshooting steps

The old page once suggested: when the description is not displayed, it can be filled in from the warning text or exception message. This recommendation no longer applies. A warning is an observation at a processing location, and exception text is another type of output; neither automatically qualifies as the object's description.

The old page also once suggested: if the reason can be displayed, the object can provisionally be assumed unchanged. This statement is appropriate only for temporarily classifying reports without an object under the display entry point. It cannot confirm the object's contents, because calling Fang Ke can convert the reason value and may display only part of it. Now, only an actual object read permits proceeding to object inspection.

These corrections did not completely rewrite the old paragraphs. The old paragraphs explain why some historical tickets retained only displayed text, and why some people later treated warnings as a source for descriptions. When reading old samples, preserve their text and observation order from that time, then add the missing markers according to the current tree, rather than disguising the old output as though the object had already been read back then.

## 2025-03-28: Corrections for empty descriptions

A later review corrected the old wording that "an empty description means information is missing". An empty description is first and foremost a read result, and should not be filled in from display text. Display text can be recorded separately as something observed by the caller, but it cannot be backfilled as the object's description; otherwise, all that remains later is a processed string, making it impossible to determine what the object originally contained.

This correction is concerned with separating two levels: what the object actually contains, and what the caller ultimately displays. In most samples, the two may be the same, so the old approach appears to work. Only when they differ is there an opportunity to determine whether the difference arose in the object, during conversion, or at the display location. Merging them prematurely removes that opportunity.

When a warning appears together with a rejection object, apply the same principle. First label which part is an object read and which part is an observation made during processing. Without these two labels, it is impossible to tell whether the report is describing the object's shape or saying that a particular caller saw a warning. Placing the warning under the object record will only obscure the empty description with text again.

If the reason value and description come from different records, still stop at the previously specified point. Even if one of the records comes from what appears to be the same caller, do not automatically assume they belong to a single read. Keep the two sources separate first, and associate them only when a shared object or shared read can be confirmed.

## Order for using the current tree

When the reporter can provide a rejection object, first read the reason value and description, note whether the description is non-empty or empty, and note whether they come from the same object. If the caller also provides the displayed result, keep that result after the object record, rather than letting it determine the field contents retroactively.

When the reporter has only display text, return to the caller that produced the text. At this point, you can record the text, the entry point, and the location where it was seen at the time, but do not make judgments about the enum or description. If an object read is later provided for the incident, add the object result alongside the original report; do not rename the earlier text as an "object value".

When the reporter sees only a pipeline warning, first record whether it was seen before, during, or after processing. If even the location is unclear, stop at the collection entry point or caller entry point, and do not label the warning as a rejection, exception, or transaction issue. Once the location is clear, continue investigating from that location, rather than first backfilling a rejection reason.

When an object is subsequently provided for the same incident, retain the object information and the warning location side by side. They can constitute observations from the same incident, but they remain two branches. Only the object read can answer questions about the value's shape; only the location where the warning was observed can support further investigation of partitioning.

When you need to read the code, you can start at `CommandProcessor` and look at nearby sections. The bindings for `ArgumentException`, `InvalidOperationException`, `GetTransactionTypeFromTransactionProvider` and `span` can all help locate where to read; they are not evidence for warning partitioning. If, after reading, you can still only say "there is an exception here" or "there is a type function here", return to the incident material and do not extend the attribution any further.

## Current object check

For callers still using this object, there is currently only one checkpoint: MessageRejectionReason preserves the RejectionReason enum value and nullable Description.

This requirement replaces the old statements "displaying it is enough" and "a null description should be filled in". It concerns what the object retains, not how callers must present text. When the description is null, record it as null; the displayed text remains a caller-side observation and cannot substitute for the object's fields.

When a caller reports that the reason value has changed, first confirm that it obtained the rejection object, then check the reason value and description. If the caller did not obtain the object, keep the issue at the display or conversion entry point rather than assuming that the object has changed. If the result of reading the object differs from the displayed result, retain both results; do not keep only the one that seems closer to the old expectation.

This checkpoint does not change the warning branch. When a warning appears, continue to record it according to whether it was observed before, during, or after processing. The two can occur in the same incident, but they cannot define the meanings of each other's fields, nor can one be declared explained just because the other is complete.

## Related issues not yet separated out

Some reports still include the transaction provider type, exception type, and rejection value shape together. The available material does not establish a causal chain linking these three. When this combination appears, first complete the object check and record the warning's location; list the transaction provider issue separately, and do not assign it to a category in the same conclusion.

Another unresolved item is: when the caller has only formatted text, which entry point is responsible for retaining the object read result. There is not enough incident material here to specify a fixed location. For now, retain the formatted text, the fact that the object was not obtained, and the caller's entry point, and continue once that entry point can be revisited.

Some older samples contain only exception names. You can start reading them at `src/Paramore.Brighter/CommandProcessor.cs`, but at present, exception names alone cannot determine whether they belong under rejection values or warning. Unless an object read or a warning location is added, keep them as unpartitioned material.

## Retained old examples

### 2023-03-20 Old example: The check passes if the reason is visible

Original text: If the reason value is displayed, that means the rejection value has not changed; if the description is not displayed, it can be filled in from the warning text.

Status: Deprecated. It mixes object reads with display results and also treats warning as a source for the description. In the same situation, follow the current object check to record whether the description is null, and retain the displayed text separately in the caller's record.

### 2023-10-25 Old example: Treat a warning near an exception as a rejection

Original text: When a warning is close to an exception, first assign it to the rejection flow, then check whether there is an object.

Status: No longer applicable. Now first confirm whether a rejection object exists; if there is no object then record only where the warning was observed. Locating the exception can still serve as a starting point for reading `CommandProcessor`, but cannot replace confirming the object.

### 2023-10-26 Old example: Finding value conversions through the transaction type function

Original text: First look at `GetTransactionTypeFromTransactionProvider`, which may explain the reason for rejection.

Status: Not substantiated. This function can still serve as a navigation point in the file, but is not listed as a troubleshooting step for rejection value shape. If direct samples become available in the future, add them under the transaction-related leads without rewriting this old example.

# Decision on Rejection Acknowledgment and Request Validation

The initial investigation tracked `negative acknowledgement action` and `request validation identity` in the same round of reliability work. Both names led the search to the area around `src/Paramore.Brighter/AsyncRequestHandlers.cs`, so the early notes treated them as two sides of one requirement.

The earlier decision was to review them together in the same batch as long as changes to the asynchronous processing entry point could explain the regression behavior for both. The main reason at the time was to avoid duplicating the investigation. There were no samples available for examining them separately, and no material that fully connected the public entry point to the handler internals.

---

Later review no longer supports the assumption that "one batch is enough to close out both." Regression follow-up has been added for RLY-206, but even after the samples were attached, an unconfirmed point remained for `negative acknowledgement action`. After RLY-222 started, the request contracts section left a separate open point for `request validation identity`. The two open items arose at different times; progress on one cannot be recorded as completion of the other.

We are switching to two records here, rather than continuing to look for a single statement that covers both.

| Item | Current tracking | Reason for retaining it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `negative acknowledgement action` | Continue checking alongside the regression follow-up for RLY-206 | One point remains unconfirmed after the samples became available |
| `request validation identity` | Continue observing via the public entry point for RLY-222 | What this entry point actually returns or throws still needs to be recorded |
| Asynchronous handler path | Retain as a lookup point from the earlier investigation | The names and call names had led the investigation here |

The earlier notes are not being discarded in full. They explain why the two names were once written together: observations were limited to the area around the handler, and no direct evidence was available at the time to distinguish them. We need to correct the completion criteria, not pretend that shared starting point never happened.

Two approaches were compared during review.
